claim: People use base rate information inconsistently in decision making.
source: Extensive evidence suggests that people use base rate information inconsistently in decision making.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, drawing from the broader literature on base rate neglect.

claim: In the inverse base rate effect (IBRE), participants classify ambiguous stimuli sharing features of both common and rare categories as members of the rare category.
source: A classic example is the inverse base rate effect (IBRE), whereby participants classify ambiguous stimuli sharing features of both common and rare categories as members of the rare category.
evidence: This is a definition of the IBRE phenomenon, supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Computational models of the IBRE have posited that it arises from associative similarity-based mechanisms.
source: Computational models of the IBRE have posited that it arises either from associative similarity-based mechanisms or from dissimilarity-based processes that may depend on higher-level inference.
evidence: This refers to existing computational models in the literature.

claim: Computational models of the IBRE have posited that it arises from dissimilarity-based processes that may depend on higher-level inference.
source: Computational models of the IBRE have posited that it arises either from associative similarity-based mechanisms or from dissimilarity-based processes that may depend on higher-level inference.
evidence: This refers to existing computational models in the literature.

claim: A hybrid model posits that similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence both contribute to the IBRE.
source: Here we develop a hybrid model, which posits that similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence both contribute to the IBRE, and test it using functional magnetic resonance imaging data collected from human subjects completing an IBRE task.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed model, which they test with fMRI data.

claim: Multivoxel pattern analysis reveals that activation patterns on ambiguous test trials contain information consistent with dissimilarity-based processing.
source: Consistent with our model, multivoxel pattern analysis reveals that activation patterns on ambiguous test trials contain information consistent with dissimilarity-based processing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: Trial-by-trial activation in left rostrolateral prefrontal cortex tracks model-based predictions for dissimilarity-based processing.
source: Further, trial-by-trial activation in left rostrolateral prefrontal cortex tracks model-based predictions for dissimilarity-based processing, consistent with theories positing a role for higher-level symbolic processing in the IBRE.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's model-based fMRI analysis.

claim: Influenza infects millions of people worldwide each year.
source: Influenza, for example, is very common and infects millions of people worldwide each year, whereas Ebola virus tends to have infection rates that are orders of magnitude lower.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about disease prevalence.

claim: Ebola virus has infection rates that are orders of magnitude lower than influenza.
source: Influenza, for example, is very common and infects millions of people worldwide each year, whereas Ebola virus tends to have infection rates that are orders of magnitude lower.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about disease prevalence.

claim: People tend to be inconsistent in their use of base rate information when making categorization decisions.
source: Research so far has suggested that people tend to be, at best, inconsistent in their use of base rate information.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of existing research findings.

claim: When confronted with examples that share characteristics with both rare and common categories, people show a tendency to predict the rare category much more often than the base rates would suggest.
source: In both realistic studies with medical professionals and artificial categorization tasks in the lab, when confronted with examples that share characteristics with both rare and common categories, people show a tendency to predict the rare category much more often than the base rates would suggest (Tversky and Kahneman, 1974; Casscells et al., 1978; Bravata, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: In the inverse base rate effect, people may predict rare categories as more likely than common ones.
source: In an extreme case, known as the inverse base rate effect (IBRE), people may even predict rare categories as more likely than common ones (Medin and Edelson, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Medin and Edelson, 1988.

claim: According to similarity-based categorization models, the IBRE arises from differential selective attention to features for common and rare categories.
source: Computationally, according to influential work with similarity-based categorization models (Medin and Edelson, 1988; Kruschke, 1996, Kruschke, 2001), the IBRE arises from differential selective attention to features for common and rare categories.
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational models in the literature.

claim: Participants learn to attend more strongly to features of rare categories, making ambiguous cases seem more similar to rare categories.
source: Specifically, participants learn to attend more strongly to features of rare categories, making ambiguous cases seem more similar to rare categories and thus more likely to be rare category members.
evidence: This is an explanation from similarity-based models cited in the literature.

claim: Model-based predictions for how similar items are to stored category representations have been shown to correlate with activation in the medial temporal lobes.
source: Model-based predictions for how similar items are to stored category representations have been shown to correlate with activation in the medial temporal lobes (MTL; Davis et al., 2012a, Davis et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Multivoxel activation patterns in the MTL contain information associated with higher-order similarity relationships between category members anticipated by similarity-based models.
source: Moreover, at a finer-grained level, multivoxel activation patterns in the MTL have been shown to contain information associated with higher-order similarity relationships between category members anticipated by similarity-based models (Davis and Poldrack, 2014), including those predicted by differences in selective attention (Mack et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) tends to track predictions of choice uncertainty from similarity-based models.
source: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) tends to track predictions of choice uncertainty from similarity-based models, whereas ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) tends to track estimates of high choice accuracy or model-confidence (Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) tends to track estimates of high choice accuracy or model-confidence.
source: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) tends to track predictions of choice uncertainty from similarity-based models, whereas ventromedial PFC (vmPFC) tends to track estimates of high choice accuracy or model-confidence (Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: People's choice of rare categories when confronted with conflicting information may stem from reliance on dissimilarity processes.
source: One alternative proposition is that people's choice of rare categories when confronted with conflicting information may stem from reliance on dissimilarity processes, either solely, or in addition to similarity-based processes.
evidence: This is an alternative theoretical proposition discussed in the literature.

claim: According to dissimilarity-based theories, people build strong expectations of the common category and view items containing features inconsistent with these expectations as more likely to be members of the rare category.
source: According to theories that focus on dissimilarity-based processes, people build strong expectations of the common category; thus they view items containing features inconsistent with these expectations as more likely to be members of the rare category (Juslin et al., 2001; Winman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to dissimilarity-based theories.

claim: ELMO argues that elimination based on dissimilarity depends on explicit reasoning processes that are separate from similarity-based processes.
source: For example, ELMO, a computational model that incorporates a choice elimination decision based on dissimilarity, argues that such elimination depends on explicit reasoning processes that are separate from similarity-based processes that arise in other trials (Juslin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the ELMO model from the cited literature.

claim: The dissGCM uses the same basic similarity computations as standard similarity-based models but allows similarities and dissimilarities to stored exemplars to be used as evidence for a category.
source: This account uses the same basic similarity computations as standard similarity-based models (e.g. Nosofsky, 1986), but allows similarities and dissimilarities to stored exemplars to be used as evidence for a category.
evidence: This is a description of the dissGCM model and its relationship to standard models.

claim: The dissGCM is agnostic about whether using dissimilarity-based evidence constitutes a different cognitive or neurobiological mechanism from using similarity-based evidence.
source: As specified computationally, the dissGCM is agnostic about whether using dissimilarity-based evidence constitutes a different cognitive or neurobiological mechanism from using similarity-based evidence.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical properties of the dissGCM model.

claim: Dissimilarity is a simple transformation of similarity in the dissGCM.
source: On one hand, the dissGCM has no fundamentally different computations from a basic similarity process; as detailed below, dissimilarity is a simple transformation of similarity.
evidence: This is a description of the computational properties of the dissGCM model.

claim: It is possible that dissimilarity processes require manipulation of similarity relationships between category representations in a more symbolic or abstract manner.
source: On the other hand, it is possible that dissimilarity processes require manipulation of similarity relationships between category representations in a more symbolic or abstract manner, as anticipated by previous dissimilarity theories.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the nature of dissimilarity processes.

claim: Higher-level cognitive control mechanisms are thought to depend on a hierarchy of abstraction in the lateral PFC along the rostral-caudal axis.
source: Higher-level cognitive control mechanisms are thought to depend on a hierarchy of abstraction in the lateral PFC along the rostral-caudal axis (Badre and D'Esposito, 2007; Badre and D'Esposito, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on PFC organization.

claim: Rostrolateral PFC (rlPFC) is often implicated in tasks that require people to generalize across abstract, symbolic representations.
source: At the apex of this hierarchy is the rostrolateral PFC (rlPFC), a region often implicated in tasks that require people to generalize across abstract, symbolic representations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about rlPFC function.

claim: Relational reasoning tasks such as Raven's progressive matrices and rule-based tasks involving abstract relations are thought to depend on left rlPFC.
source: For example, relational reasoning tasks such as Raven's progressive matrices and rule-based tasks involving abstract relations are thought to depend on left rlPFC (Christoff et al., 2001; Bunge et al., 2005, Bunge et al., 2009; Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on rlPFC function.

claim: Left rlPFC is involved in rule evaluation and novel generalization processes for simpler feature-based rules in categorization tasks.
source: In addition to its role in generalizing abstract, relational rules, we have recently found left rlPFC to be involved in rule evaluation and novel generalization processes for simpler feature-based rules in categorization tasks (Paniukov and Davis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Dissimilarity-based generalization to novel feature pairings may depend on rule evaluation processes in the rlPFC more so than simple similarity-based processing.
source: In the present study, dissimilarity-based generalization to novel feature pairings may depend on rule evaluation processes in the rlPFC more so than simple similarity-based processing, if studies anticipating that dissimilarity-based processes depend more upon higher-level symbolic rules are correct (Juslin et al., 2001; Winman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous dissimilarity-based theories.

claim: Pure similarity-based accounts suggest that generalization patterns in an IBRE task do not depend on the existence of a separate, higher-level mechanism.
source: Alternatively, pure similarity-based accounts suggest that generalization patterns in an IBRE task do not depend on the existence of a separate, higher-level mechanism (Medin and Edelson, 1988; Kruschke, 1996, Kruschke, 2001), and would thus expect a single neurobiological network associated with similarity-based processing to be engaged for choice across trials.
evidence: This is a prediction from similarity-based theories cited in the literature.

claim: Real world visual categories faces, scenes, and objects have a well-defined representational topography across the cortex.
source: These visual categories have a well-defined representational topography across the cortex (Haxby et al., 2001; Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014), allowing us to predict whether participants are differentially activating particular stimulus features (faces, scenes, or objects) by computing similarities between activation patterns elicited for the key IBRE trials and feature-specific patterns from an independent localizer scan.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging research.

claim: The dissGCM predicts greater contributions from the common, unchosen category during the retrieval process on ambiguous trials.
source: Because the dissGCM predicts greater contributions from the common, unchosen category during this retrieval process, we expect multivoxel patterns during ambiguous trials to reveal greater activation of information associated with the common, unchosen category.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the dissGCM model.

claim: All subjects reached greater than 90% accuracy over the last four blocks of learning.
source: All subjects reached greater than 90% accuracy over the last four blocks (M = 98.1%, SD = 2.4%, range = 93.5–100%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study's data.

claim: Mean choice performance in the first block was above chance (25%) for both common and rare feature pairs.
source: Mean choice performance in the first block was above chance (25%) for both common (M = 63.6%) and rare (M = 43.2%) feature pairs.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study's data.

claim: A linear mixed effects model revealed a significant block by trial type interaction, suggesting that the common diseases were learned more quickly than the rare diseases.
source: Consistent with previous IBRE studies, a linear mixed effects model revealed a significant block by trial type interaction (F (1, 262)=20.7, p<0.001), suggesting that the common diseases were learned more quickly than the rare diseases.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data analysis.

claim: Participants were significantly more accurate on common compared with rare disease trials in the first, second, third, fourth, and 12th blocks.
source: Paired t-tests revealed that participants were significantly more accurate on common compared with rare disease trials in the first (t (21)=2.26, p=0.034), second (t (21)=2.85, p=0.010), third (t (21)=2.72, p=0.013), fourth (t (21)=2.46, p=0.023), and 12th blocks (t (21)=2.23, p=0.037).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data analysis.

claim: Participants were numerically more likely to classify ambiguous test stimuli as members of the relevant rare category (M = 49.8%) than the relevant common category (M = 43.5%).
source: Consistent with an inverse base rate effect, participants were numerically more likely to classify ambiguous test stimuli (combinations of rare and common features) as members of the relevant rare category (M = 49.8%) than the relevant common category (M = 43.5%) combined across object-scene, scene-scene, and object-object pairs.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study's test phase data.

claim: The percentage of rare responding on ambiguous trials was significantly higher than the 1/4 base rate for the rare category.
source: A one-sample t-test revealed that the percentage of rare responding on ambiguous trials was significantly higher than the 1/4 base rate for the rare category (t (21)=8.11, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's test phase data.

claim: Participants chose the rare category for ambiguous pairs significantly more often than for the imperfect predictors (faces: M = 30.0%).
source: Likewise, participants chose the rare category for ambiguous pairs significantly more often than for the imperfect predictors (faces: M = 30.0%), (t (21)=3.85, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's test phase data.

claim: RTs were slower when participants made rare responses (M = 1.47 s) than common responses (M = 1.27 s) on ambiguous test trials.
source: On these trials of interest, a linear mixed effects model revealed that RTs were slower when participants made rare responses (M = 1.47 s) than common responses (M = 1.27 s), (t (21)=10.48, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study's test phase data.

claim: The observation of slowed RTs on ambiguous trials receiving rare responses suggests that rare selections may be more cognitively demanding relative to common selections.
source: The observation of slowed RTs on ambiguous trials receiving rare responses suggests that rare selections may be more cognitively demanding relative to common selections, consistent with previous dissimilarity-based theories of IBRE that posit a role of higher-level, inferential reasoning in base rate neglect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RT data, consistent with dissimilarity-based theories.

claim: When examining how much each category's exemplars contributed to the rare response for ambiguous items, the model posits that rare choices are more probable because of the contribution that dissimilarity to the common category makes to the evidence for the rare category relative to the contribution of similarity to the rare category.
source: When examining how much each category's exemplars (common and rare) contributed to the rare response for ambiguous items, the model posits that rare choices are more probable because of the contribution that dissimilarity to the common category makes to the evidence for the rare category relative to the contribution of similarity to the rare category.
evidence: This is a prediction from the dissGCM model.

claim: In the fitted version of the model, the proportion of the overall evidence for rare contributed by similarity to the rare category exemplar was nearly half the evidence contributed by dissimilarity to the common category exemplar (rare = 0.088; common = 0.153).
source: For example, using these formulas, in the fitted version of the model, the proportion of the overall evidence for rare contributed by similarity to the rare category exemplar was nearly half the evidence contributed by dissimilarity to the common category exemplar (rare = 0.088; common = 0.153, in the dissGCM's attention weighted similarity units).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Pattern estimates discriminated between information associated with control items during test: pattern similarity estimates for objects were significantly greater on object-only trials than scene-only trials.
source: Pattern estimates were found to discriminate between information associated with control items during test: pattern similarity estimates for objects were significantly greater on object-only trials (O1, O2, and O1+O2) than scene-only trials (S1, S2, and S1+S2), (t (21)=2.83, p=0.010), and vice versa (t (21)=5.60, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: Estimates for faces on face-only control trials were significantly greater than on object-only trials and scene-only trials.
source: Likewise, estimates for faces on face-only control trials were found to be significantly greater than on object-only trials (t (21)=2.54, p=0.019), and scene-only trials (t (21)=2.92, p=0.008).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: A linear mixed effects model revealed a significant interaction between response and pattern similarity to common and rare features, whereby participants tended to more strongly activate patterns associated with common features only when they made a rare response.
source: Consistent with the dissGCM's predictions, a linear mixed effects model with BOLD pattern similarity as the outcome variable and categorical predictors for response, stimulus dimension (common vs. rare), and visual stimulus category (objects vs. scenes) revealed a significant interaction between response and pattern similarity to common and rare features, whereby participants tended to more strongly activate patterns associated with common features only when they made a rare response (F (1, 42)=4.92, p=0.032).
evidence: This is a primary result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: When participants chose the rare category, their activation patterns were most similar to whichever visual stimulus category (scenes or objects) was associated with the common category.
source: Specifically, when participants chose the rare category, their activation patterns were most similar to whichever visual stimulus category (scenes or objects) was associated with the common category (t (21)=2.78, p=0.011).
evidence: This is a primary result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference between pattern similarity for rare and common features when participants made a common response.
source: Interestingly, there was no significant difference between pattern similarity for rare and common features when participants made a common response (t (21)=0.45, p=0.653).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: Visual stimulus category was not found to interact with response or whether an item was rare or common in the pattern similarity model.
source: Visual stimulus category was not found to interact with response (F (1, 72)=0.229, p=0.634), or whether an item was rare or common (F (1, 72)=0.241, p=0.625), in the pattern similarity model, and thus the results in Figure 3 are collapsed across objects and scenes.
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: A one-sample t-test revealed no significant differences in pattern similarity to the face dimension across responses.
source: However, a one-sample t-test revealed no significant differences in pattern similarity to the face dimension across responses (t (21)=0.22, p=0.828).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: Bayes factors suggested positive evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for pattern similarity on common response trials (BF01 = 7.54).
source: Bayes factors for each of these hypotheses were tested using the BIC approximation method, computing exp(ΔBIC/2) between the null and alternative models (Wagenmakers, 2007). The resulting Bayes factors suggested positive evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for pattern similarity on common response trials (BF01 = 7.54), and conversely, positive evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis that common features would be more strongly represented on rare response trials (BF10 = 4.36).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian analysis of the multivoxel data.

claim: Bayes factors suggested positive evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis that common features would be more strongly represented on rare response trials (BF10 = 4.36).
source: Bayes factors for each of these hypotheses were tested using the BIC approximation method, computing exp(ΔBIC/2) between the null and alternative models (Wagenmakers, 2007). The resulting Bayes factors suggested positive evidence in favor of the null hypothesis for pattern similarity on common response trials (BF01 = 7.54), and conversely, positive evidence in favor of the alternative hypothesis that common features would be more strongly represented on rare response trials (BF10 = 4.36).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian analysis of the multivoxel data.

claim: The multivoxel results point to the existence of a distinct process for common responses that is, on average, less dependent on the activation of common or rare category exemplars.
source: Accordingly, beyond revealing that a dissimilarity-based process contributes to rare responding in an IBRE task, our multivoxel results point to the existence of a distinct process for common responses that is, on average, less dependent on the activation of common or rare category exemplars.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multivoxel pattern analysis results.

claim: Both similarity-based models and dissimilarity-based models such as the dissGCM predict that features which are most informative about the correct category will contribute more to categorization decisions during learning.
source: Generally, both similarity-based models and dissimilarity-based models such as the dissGCM predict that features which are most informative about the correct category will contribute more to categorization decisions during learning.
evidence: This is a prediction from both types of models.

claim: A linear mixed effects model collapsed across trial type revealed that pattern similarity to the visual category was the strongest for perfectly predictive features (M = .065), followed by the non-predictive but present features (M = −0.050) and the non-present features (M = −0.145).
source: As anticipated, a linear mixed effects model collapsed across trial type revealed that pattern similarity to the visual category was the strongest for perfectly predictive features (M = .065), followed by the non-predictive but present features (M = −0.050) and the non-present features (M = −0.145), (F (2, 42)=54.8, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis of the learning phase.

claim: For common trials, pairwise comparisons revealed significant differences between pattern similarity to perfect and imperfect predictors, perfect predictors and non-present features, and between imperfect predictors and non-present features.
source: For common trials, pairwise comparisons revealed significant differences between pattern similarity to perfect and imperfect predictors (t (21)=3.38, p=0.003), perfect predictors and non-present features (t (21)=5.71, p<0.001), and between imperfect predictors and non-present features (t (21)=4.27, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis of the learning phase.

claim: For rare trials, significant differences were found between pattern similarity to perfect and imperfect predictors, perfect predictors and non-present features, and between imperfect predictors and non-present features.
source: Likewise, for rare trials we found significant differences between pattern similarity to perfect and imperfect predictors (t (21)=5.69, p<0.001), perfect predictors and non-present features (t (21)=9.11, p<0.001), and between imperfect predictors and non-present features in the expected directions (t (21)=3.11, p=0.005) (see Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis of the learning phase.

claim: Greater activation of multivoxel patterns associated with common perfect predictors during learning was correlated with a higher proportion of rare choices on the ambiguous test trials (r = 0.590).
source: Consistent with dissimilarity-based accounts, we found that greater activation of multivoxel patterns associated with common perfect predictors during learning was correlated with a higher proportion of rare choices on the ambiguous test trials (r = 0.590, t (20)=3.27, p=0.004).
evidence: This is a correlation result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: No significant relationship was found between activation of multivoxel patterns during learning and choice proportions on IBRE trials for rare perfect predictors.
source: Alternatively, we found no significant relationship between activation of multivoxel patterns during learning and choice proportions on IBRE trials for rare perfect predictors (r = 0.114, t (20)=0.512, p=0.614), common faces (r = −0.163, t (20)=−0.737, p=0.470), or rare faces (r = −0.039, t (20)=−0.173, p=0.865).
evidence: This is a correlation result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: A linear mixed effects model revealed an interaction between pattern similarity to different learning phase items and base rate neglect.
source: A linear mixed effects model including factors for each item and participants' rare choice proportions was used to test for significant differences in slope among the above associations. The model revealed an interaction between pattern similarity to different learning phase items and base rate neglect (F (3, 60)=2.97, p=0.039).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: The relationship between pattern similarity to common perfect predictors and base rate neglect was stronger, in the positive direction, than those for common faces and rare faces.
source: Specifically, the relationship between pattern similarity to common perfect predictors and base rate neglect was stronger, in the positive direction, than those for common faces (t (60)=2.72, p=0.009), and rare faces (t (60)=2.40, p=0.020).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: The difference in positive slope between pattern similarity and base rate neglect for common versus rare perfect predictors was marginally significant.
source: Likewise, the difference in positive slope between pattern similarity and base rate neglect for common versus rare perfect predictors was marginally significant (t (60)=1.88, p=0.065).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the multivoxel pattern analysis.

claim: Greater similarity-based contributions to the winning category were associated with activation in the MTL (left hippocampus), vmPFC, and primary motor cortex.
source: Our analysis showed that greater similarity-based contributions to the winning category were associated with activation in the MTL (left hippocampus) vmPFC, and primary motor cortex (Figure 6A, depicted in red; Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the model-based univariate fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The engagement of vmPFC corroborates recent studies suggesting that this region tracks higher relative evidence for categorization decisions.
source: Likewise, the engagement of vmPFC corroborates recent studies suggesting that this region tracks higher relative evidence for categorization decisions (Davis et al., 2017; O'Bryan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in the context of previous research.

claim: The positive relationship between vmPFC and similarity processes may be reflective of attention to strong predictors or the application of familiar category rules.
source: The positive relationship between vmPFC and similarity processes may also be reflective of attention to strong predictors (Sharpe and Killcross, 2015; Nasser et al., 2017) or the application of familiar category rules (Boettiger and D'Esposito, 2005; Liu et al., 2015), both of which are consistent with similarity-based accounts of IBRE that attribute choice to a well-established association between perfect predictors and their outcomes that is driven by attention (e.g. Kruschke, 1996).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in the context of previous research.

claim: Primary motor cortex has been found to track increasing levels of response automaticity in categorization tasks.
source: While more anterior motor-planning regions such as pre-SMA and SMA tend to be associated with rule acquisition processes (e.g. Boettiger and D'Esposito, 2005), primary motor cortex has been found to track increasing levels of response automaticity in categorization tasks (Waldschmidt and Ashby, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The dlPFC, dorsomedial PFC, and posterior parietal cortex were found to be negatively correlated with similarity-based evidence for the chosen category.
source: The dlPFC, dorsomedial PFC, and posterior parietal cortex were found to be negatively correlated with similarity-based evidence for the chosen category (Figure 6A, depicted in blue; Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the model-based univariate fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The fronto-parietal network is generally associated with rule-based category learning.
source: This fronto-parietal network is generally associated with rule-based category learning (Filoteo et al., 2005; Seger and Cincotta, 2006; Soto et al., 2013), and is thought to play a critical role in representing the uncertainty associated with categorization decisions (DeGutis and D'Esposito, 2007; Seger et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The fronto-parietal network is thought to play a critical role in representing the uncertainty associated with categorization decisions.
source: This fronto-parietal network is generally associated with rule-based category learning (Filoteo et al., 2005; Seger and Cincotta, 2006; Soto et al., 2013), and is thought to play a critical role in representing the uncertainty associated with categorization decisions (DeGutis and D'Esposito, 2007; Seger et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The results suggest that dlPFC and functionally related fronto-parietal regions may be engaged in cases where probes fail to elicit a strong similarity-based match with stored category exemplars.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with these findings, and moreover, suggest that dlPFC and functionally related fronto-parietal regions may be engaged in cases where probes fail to elicit a strong similarity-based match with stored category exemplars.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Dissimilarity-based evidence was positively correlated with activation in the left rlPFC.
source: Contrastingly, dissimilarity-based evidence was positively correlated with activation in the left rlPFC (Figure 6B; Table 2), consistent with our hypothesis that this type of evidence might encourage more symbolic processes believed to underlie the rlPFC's contribution to category learning (Davis et al., 2017; Paniukov and Davis, 2018).
evidence: This is a result from the model-based univariate fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: No clusters were significantly negatively associated with dissimilarity-based evidence.
source: No clusters were significantly negatively associated with dissimilarity-based evidence.
evidence: This is a result from the model-based univariate fMRI analysis.

claim: Greater relative contributions of dissimilarity-based evidence do not necessitate smaller contributions of similarity-based evidence in the dissGCM.
source: Comparing the statistical maps in Figure 6A and B, it is apparent that greater relative contributions of dissimilarity-based evidence do not necessitate smaller contributions of similarity-based evidence in the dissGCM: if these regressors were anticorrelated, one would expect the regions associated with dissimilarity processes to resemble the fronto-parietal network we found to be negatively associated with similarity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the fMRI results in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: All three maps (positive similarity, negative similarity, and positive dissimilarity) revealed significant activation in portions of ventral occipitotemporal cortex.
source: Despite obvious differences between the activation patterns elicited for each contrast, it is notable that all three maps (positive similarity, negative similarity, and positive dissimilarity) revealed significant activation in portions of ventral occipitotemporal cortex.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ventral occipitotemporal regions (lateral occipital cortex, inferior temporal gyrus, and fusiform gyrus) have well-established roles in representing visual object categories.
source: These regions (lateral occipital cortex, inferior temporal gyrus, and fusiform gyrus) have well-established roles in representing visual object categories, including those used as stimulus dimensions in the present study (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The engagement of ventral occipitotemporal regions may reflect feature-based attention, exemplar retrieval, or a combination of both processes.
source: Accordingly, it is possible that the engagement of these regions in our study reflects feature-based attention, exemplar retrieval, or a combination of both processes that occurs regardless of the respective contributions that similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence make to a decision.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Multivoxel analysis suggested stronger activation of patterns associated with features of the common category when participants classified ambiguous stimuli as rare.
source: First, as predicted by the dissGCM's relative contribution of similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence during the ambiguous trials, multivoxel analysis suggested stronger activation of patterns associated with features of the common category when participants classified ambiguous stimuli as rare.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary multivoxel pattern analysis finding.

claim: Model-based univariate analysis revealed that measures of similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence had unique neural topographies.
source: Second, model-based univariate analysis revealed that measures of similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence had unique neural topographies.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary univariate fMRI finding.

claim: Dissimilarity-based processes can be viewed as simple extensions of similarity-based processing and need not depend on the existence of a functionally separate categorization system.
source: As illustrated by the dissGCM, such dissimilarity-based processes can be viewed as simple extensions of similarity-based processing and need not depend on the existence of a functionally separate categorization system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dissGCM model's theoretical implications.

claim: Neuroimaging results suggest that dissimilarity, but not similarity-based evidence may arise from processing in rlPFC regions that are known to be involved with higher-level reasoning and problem solving.
source: At the same time, our neuroimaging results suggest that dissimilarity, but not similarity-based evidence may arise from processing in rlPFC regions that are known to be involved with higher-level reasoning and problem solving (Christoff et al., 2001; Bunge et al., 2005, Bunge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI results in the context of previous research.

claim: One possibility for reconciling theories is that the dissimilarity-based evidence involves more abstract or symbolic feature processing than pure similarity processes, and this additional processing taps rlPFC regions.
source: One possibility for reconciling these theories is that the dissimilarity-based evidence involves more abstract or symbolic feature processing than pure similarity processes, and this additional processing taps rlPFC regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: rlPFC tracks measures of relational encoding in category learning.
source: This is consistent with our recent model-based fMRI results, which demonstrate that rlPFC tracks measures of relational encoding in category learning, but otherwise this type of category learning may rely on the same basic similarity-based mechanisms as simpler feature-based learning (Davis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: A common thread among tasks shown to engage the rlPFC is that they tend to involve combining across disparate representations to form the basis for a decision.
source: A common thread among tasks shown to engage the rlPFC is that they tend to involve combining across disparate representations to form the basis for a decision – whether those representations comprise confidence estimates and subjective value (De Martino et al., 2013), visual features and their relations (Bunge, 2004; Bunge et al., 2009; Davis et al., 2017), or expected rewards and their relative uncertainties (Boorman et al., 2009; Badre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on rlPFC function.

claim: The involvement of rlPFC when participants place more reliance on dissimilarity-based evidence may be attributable to increasing demands for integrating evidence across several abstract representations.
source: Although the dissGCM instantiates dissimilarity as a simple transformation of similarity, the involvement of rlPFC when participants place more reliance on dissimilarity-based evidence may be attributable to increasing demands for integrating evidence across several abstract representations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the rlPFC findings.

claim: Recent findings implicate the rlPFC in evaluative processes for categorization tasks that require candidate rules to be weighed over the course of several trials.
source: This hypothesis accords with recent findings implicating the rlPFC in evaluative processes for categorization tasks that require candidate rules to be weighed over the course of several trials, relative to matching tasks where a rule can be known with certainty following a single correct trial (Paniukov and Davis, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: When viewed through the lens of basic similarity-based attentional processes, the IBRE appears to arise from very simple learning mechanisms that are not particularly tied to higher-level rationality.
source: When viewed through the lens of basic similarity-based attentional processes (e.g. Medin and Edelson, 1988; Kruschke, 1996, Kruschke, 2001), the IBRE appears to arise from very simple learning mechanisms that are not particularly tied to higher-level rationality, and rare choices seem to indicate a lack of knowledge of the base rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of similarity-based theories of IBRE.

claim: The standard GCM was only able to predict a greater proportion of rare choices if accurate knowledge of the exemplar base rates was eliminated.
source: Indeed, in a separate model fit, we attempted to fit the standard similarity-based GCM to the key pattern on the ambiguous trials. However, the standard GCM was only able to predict a greater proportion of rare choices if accurate knowledge of the exemplar base rates was eliminated (all values of tj = 1 or fit as free parameters).
evidence: This is a result from an additional model fitting analysis.

claim: In the dissGCM, accurate knowledge of the category base rates directly contributes to the greater dissimilarity-based evidence against the common category.
source: In contrast, accurate knowledge of the category base rates directly contributes to the greater dissimilarity-based evidence against the common category.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the dissGCM differs from the standard GCM.

claim: From the dissGCM perspective, participants are perfectly knowledgeable about the base rates in the present task, but they use this knowledge in a way not anticipated by pure similarity-based models.
source: Thus from the dissGCM perspective, participants are perfectly knowledgeable about the base rates in the present task, but they use this knowledge in a way not anticipated by pure similarity-based models.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dissGCM model's implications.

claim: The dissGCM was originally developed to explain sequential effects in categorization.
source: The dissGCM was originally developed to explain sequential effects in categorization (Stewart and Morin, 2007), and its success in this domain suggests that dissimilarity processes, such as those revealed here, may be present in many categorization tasks that are more familiar in the neuroimaging literature.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original dissGCM paper.

claim: Purely attentional accounts posit that strong initial learning of the common category leads people to learn the rare category by the features that distinguish it from the common.
source: For example, purely attentional accounts posit that strong initial learning of the common category leads people to learn the rare category by the features that distinguish it from the common (Markman, 1989; Kruschke, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to attentional theories of IBRE.

claim: Learning-order effects play a role in the IBRE: previous studies have shown that using blocked or unequally distributed category frequencies during training leads participants to favor later-learned categories on ambiguous test probes.
source: Learning-order effects do appear to play a role in the IBRE: previous studies have shown that using blocked or unequally distributed category frequencies during training leads participants to favor later-learned categories on ambiguous test probes, even when overall base rates are held constant (Medin and Bettger, 1991; Kruschke, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on learning order effects.

claim: In blocked learning, categories are learned by viewing a number of items from the same category before switching to other categories.
source: In blocked learning, categories are learned by viewing a number of items from the same category before switching to other categories.
evidence: This is a definition of blocked learning.

claim: In interleaved learning, items from all categories are presented in a random order such that the examples of the different categories are intermixed.
source: In interleaved learning, the standard for category learning, items from all categories are presented in a random order such that the examples of the different categories are intermixed.
evidence: This is a definition of interleaved learning.

claim: Blocked learning tends to lead participants to focus more on stimulus features that are shared with members of the same category, whereas interleaved learning tends to lead participants to focus more on features that differentiate categories.
source: Blocked learning tends to lead participants to focus more on stimulus features that are shared with members of the same category, whereas interleaved learning tends to lead participants to focus more on features that differentiate categories.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about blocked vs. interleaved learning.

claim: Frequency manipulations such as those used in the present study have an effect of creating more blocking within common categories and interleaving within rare categories.
source: Interestingly, while not an interleaved versus blocked manipulation per se, frequency manipulations such as those used in the present study have an effect of creating more blocking within common categories – common categories are more likely to follow examples of the same category, and interleaving within rare categories.
evidence: This is an inference about the properties of the experimental design.

claim: Formal computational models of blocked versus interleaved learning have focused on how these scenarios produce differences in selective attention to stimulus features that are characteristic (blocked) or diagnostic (interleaved) of a category, and are pure similarity-based models such as the original GCM.
source: However, formal computational models of blocked versus interleaved learning have thus far focused on how these scenarios produce differences in selective attention to stimulus features that are characteristic (blocked) or diagnostic (interleaved) of a category, and are pure similarity-based models such as the original GCM (Carvalho and Goldstone, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous modeling work.

claim: MVPA and univariate fMRI results show that pure similarity-based processing cannot fully explain the IBRE.
source: Contrastingly, our MVPA and univariate fMRI results show that pure similarity-based processing cannot fully explain the IBRE, and thus strongly suggest that dissimilarity processes contribute to the IBRE.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's fMRI results.

claim: The dissGCM, like the standard GCM, is a model of asymptotic categorization performance and generalization, and thus is not well-equipped to account for learning dynamics or individual differences.
source: The dissGCM, like the standard GCM, is a model of asymptotic categorization performance and generalization, and thus is not well-equipped to account for learning dynamics or individual differences.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the dissGCM model.

claim: Dissimilarity-based theories posit that one of the reasons IBRE arises is because the common category becomes more thoroughly established in memory during learning, which leads participants to retrieve this information more readily at test.
source: Dissimilarity-based theories posit that one of the reasons IBRE arises is because the common category becomes more thoroughly established in memory during learning, which leads participants to retrieve this information more readily at test.
evidence: This is a summary of dissimilarity-based theories.

claim: Participants who learn the common category more strongly should exhibit base rate neglect more frequently, according to dissimilarity-based theories.
source: From this perspective, participants who learn the common category more strongly should consequently exhibit base rate neglect more frequently.
evidence: This is a prediction from dissimilarity-based theories.

claim: Pattern similarity analyses revealed that participants who more strongly activated information associated with common categories during learning engaged in base rate neglect more often at test.
source: Consistent with these predictions of dissimilarity-based theories, pattern similarity analyses revealed that participants who more strongly activated information associated with common categories during learning engaged in base rate neglect more often at test.
evidence: This is a result from the individual differences analysis.

claim: Individual differences in learning contribute to IBRE.
source: While these results suggest that individual differences in learning contribute to IBRE, they nonetheless point to a critical need to develop a full learning-based version of the dissGCM that can be applied at the individual level to capture these differences.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the individual differences results.

claim: One possibility is that participants' weighting of similarity and dissimilarity (the s parameter) changes over learning based on the participants' learning rates and factors related to blocking versus interleaved presentation.
source: For example, one possibility is that participants' weighting of similarity and dissimilarity (the s parameter) changes over learning based on the participants' learning rates and factors related to blocking versus interleaved presentation (Carvalho and Goldstone, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about how the dissGCM could be extended.

claim: Multivoxel patterns associated with predictive features were more strongly activated than imperfectly predictive features during the learning phase.
source: Consistent with past research using MVPA to decode learned selective attention (Mack et al., 2013, Mack et al., 2016; Leong et al., 2017; O'Bryan et al., 2018), multivoxel patterns associated with predictive features were more strongly activated than imperfectly predictive features during the learning phase.
evidence: This is a result from the multivoxel pattern analysis of the learning phase.

claim: Rare category selections were accompanied by slower RTs relative to common selections.
source: Moreover, rare category selections were accompanied by slower RTs relative to common selections.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the study.

claim: It is possible that participants are more likely to respond according to the base rates when the ambiguous stimuli elicit a strong similarity-based match.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that participants are more likely to respond according to the base rates when the ambiguous stimuli elicit a strong similarity-based match: given our RT results along with the correlation between similarity-based evidence and motor cortex engagement, in these cases subjects may revert to habitual response patterns from the learning phase and simply choose the more well-established (common) category.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The observed attention weight parameters wk from the model fits are consistent with greater selective attention allocated to the rare feature dimension.
source: Interestingly, while our findings argue against the prediction from similarity-based models that the IBRE arises because rare features become more similar to their associated category, the observed attention weight parameters wk from the model fits are consistent with a key part of similarity theory – that there is greater selective attention allocated to the rare feature dimension.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: The rare feature dimensions outweighed the common features for both sets of categories in the data.
source: Indeed, the rare feature dimensions outweighed the common features for both sets of categories in our data.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: The larger attention weights for rare features did not drive greater pattern similarity to the rare feature dimension in the multivoxel results.
source: However, these larger attention weights did not seem to drive greater pattern similarity to the rare feature dimension in our multivoxel results.
evidence: This is an observation about the relationship between model parameters and multivoxel results.

claim: The multivoxel results are predicted to indicate some combination of attention and memory-based retrieval of the category exemplars.
source: We predict that our multivoxel results are not driven directly by simple feature-based attention, but instead indicate some combination of attention and memory-based retrieval of the category exemplars.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the multivoxel pattern similarity measures reflect.

claim: Pattern similarity measures in ventral temporal cortex have been shown to effectively index both dimensional selective attention and the retrieval of non-present, associated stimuli.
source: Pattern similarity measures in ventral temporal cortex have been shown to effectively index both dimensional selective attention (Leong et al., 2017; O'Bryan et al., 2018) and the retrieval of non-present, associated stimuli (e.g. Zeithamova et al., 2012; for review, see Rissman and Wagner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A possibility that accords with both attention and memory explanations is that pattern similarity indices reflect information that is actively represented in working memory.
source: Rather than adjudicating between whether the multivoxel patterns in the current study are more likely to indicate attention or memory, a possibility that accords with both potential explanations is that these pattern similarity indices reflect information that is actively represented in working memory, either by way of visual cueing or reinstated long-term memories (Lewis-Peacock and Postle, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: In cases in which multiple or competing stimulus representations are present in working memory, multivoxel patterns should be most similar to whichever representation is consciously attended.
source: In cases in which multiple or competing stimulus representations are present in WM, as may be expected for the ambiguous IBRE trials, multivoxel patterns should be most similar to whichever representation is consciously attended (Lewis-Peacock et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Using model-based fMRI analysis, evidence was found that extreme cases of base rate neglect such as the IBRE may arise from a combination of similarity- and dissimilarity-based processes.
source: In conclusion, using model-based fMRI analysis, we found evidence that extreme cases of base rate neglect such as the IBRE may arise from a combination of similarity- and dissimilarity-based processes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Measures of neural activation suggest that people may be more strongly relying on evidence about how dissimilar an item is to common categories when faced with ambiguous stimuli.
source: Accordingly, measures of neural activation suggest that people may be more strongly relying on evidence about how dissimilar an item is to common categories when faced with ambiguous stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Dissimilarity processes have a unique cortical topography that includes the rostrolateral PFC.
source: Furthermore, dissimilarity processes have a unique cortical topography that includes the rostrolateral PFC, a region believed to be involved with more symbolic feature processing.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: Twenty-four healthy right-handed volunteers participated in the study.
source: Twenty-four healthy right-handed volunteers (age range 18–58; 13 women) participated in the study for $35.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Two participants were excluded, one for falling asleep and the other for registration failures in the first five scanning runs.
source: Two participants were excluded, one for falling asleep and the other for registration failures in the first five scanning runs.
evidence: This is a description of participant exclusions.

claim: All protocols were approved by the Texas Tech University IRB.
source: All protocols were approved by the Texas Tech University IRB.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The study consisted of three phases: localizer, learning, and test.
source: The study consisted of three phases: localizer, learning, and test.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The localizer phase consisted of two scanning runs in which participants classified images based on whether they contained a face, an object, or a scene.
source: The localizer phase consisted of two scanning runs (run length = 5 min 10 s) in which participants classified images based on whether they contained a face, an object, or a scene.
evidence: This is a description of the localizer phase procedure.

claim: Over the duration of the localizer phase, subjects categorized 38 examples of each stimulus type.
source: Over the duration of the localizer phase, subjects categorized 38 examples of each stimulus type.
evidence: This is a description of the localizer phase procedure.

claim: In the learning phase, participants learned a classic IBRE category structure.
source: In the learning phase, participants learned a classic IBRE category structure (Medin and Edelson, 1988; see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the learning phase procedure, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Faces were always assigned to the imperfectly predictive feature dimensions, whereas objects and scenes were perfectly predictive and associated with only one disease.
source: Faces were always assigned to the imperfectly predictive feature dimensions, whereas objects and scenes were perfectly predictive and associated with only one disease (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The learning phase was spread over three scanning runs, and four blocks of the stimulus set were presented per run, resulting in a total of 12 blocks and 96 trials for the learning phase.
source: The learning phase was spread over three scanning runs (run length = 5 min 10 s), and four blocks of the stimulus set were presented per run, resulting in a total of 12 blocks and 96 trials for the learning phase.
evidence: This is a description of the learning phase procedure.

claim: During the test phase, participants completed trials with both new and old exemplars and classified them without receiving feedback.
source: During the test phase, participants completed trials with both new and old exemplars and classified them as 'Disease 1, 2, 3, or 4?', but no longer received feedback.
evidence: This is a description of the test phase procedure.

claim: The test phase occurred over three consecutive scanning runs.
source: Like the learning phase, the test phase occurred over three consecutive scanning runs (run length = 5 min 10 s).
evidence: This is a description of the test phase procedure.

claim: Each item in the stimulus set was encountered twice per run during the test phase, with the exception of the ambiguous perfect predictor pairs which were repeated four times per run.
source: Each item in the stimulus set was encountered twice per run, with the exception of the ambiguous perfect predictor pairs which were repeated four times per run.
evidence: This is a description of the test phase procedure.

claim: This resulted in 24 instances of ambiguous scene-object pairs, and 48 instances of the ambiguous trials overall for each participant.
source: This resulted in 24 instances of ambiguous scene-object pairs, and 48 instances of the ambiguous trials overall for each participant.
evidence: This is a description of the test phase procedure.

claim: The dissGCM is an extension of the generalized context model that accounts for choice using a combination of similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence.
source: The dissimilarity generalized context model (dissGCM; Stewart and Morin, 2007) is an extension of the generalized context model (Nosofsky, 1986) that accounts for choice using a combination of similarity- and dissimilarity-based evidence.
evidence: This is a description of the dissGCM model.

claim: In the dissGCM, stimuli are represented as points in a multidimensional feature space.
source: Like the original GCM, stimuli are represented as points in a multidimensional feature space.
evidence: This is a description of the dissGCM model.

claim: The model was fit to the group response frequencies for each option by minimizing the −2 * Log Likelihood using a differential evolution function optimizer.
source: The model was fit to the group response frequencies for each option by minimizing the −2 * Log Likelihood using a differential evolution function optimizer.
evidence: This is a description of the model fitting procedure.

claim: The overall fit of the model was 4,314.588.
source: The overall fit was 4,314.588.
evidence: This is a result from the model fitting procedure.

claim: Imaging data were acquired on a 3.0 T Siemens Skyra MRI scanner at the Texas Tech Neuroimaging Institute.
source: Imaging data were acquired on a 3.0 T Siemens Skyra MRI scanner at the Texas Tech Neuroimaging Institute.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging acquisition parameters.

claim: Functional data were preprocessed and analyzed using FSL.
source: Functional data were preprocessed and analyzed using FSL (www.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

source: For the model-based univariate analysis, functional images were spatially smoothed using a 6 mm FWHM Gaussian kernel.
evidence: This is a description of the data preprocessing methods.

claim: No smoothing was performed on functional data used for the multivoxel analysis.
source: No smoothing was performed on functional data used for the multivoxel analysis.

source: RSA was conducted using the PyMVPA toolbox (Hanke et al., 2009) and custom Python routines.

source: Source data and scripts used to create all figures and tables (e.g. R code, PyMVPA scripts, statistical maps for the model-based fMRI analysis) are freely available online at https://osf.io/atbz7/.
